Observation Details: Photos.  First found by the Voltz's (Peggy & Jim) at approximately 1 p.m. today.    This is not when and where I expected to see the first limpkin recorded in Buchanan County.  It was on S50th Street on the east side of the Missouri Western State University campus.  It was walking around a small puddle along the edge of the road & in the road itself at the entrance the the maintenance sheds between a dorm parking lot to the south & the small parking lot for the John Rushin Teaching & Research Prairie Reconstruction to the north.  I occasionally saw it pecking at debris in the road but never actually saw it eat anything.  Four vehicles drove by while I was observing the bird from the dorm parking lot entrance to the south.  Each time, the bird moved to the side of the road & returned to the puddle edge & the road itself after the vehicles had passed.  The nearest permanent bodies of water are a small pond on campus (~2 acres) ~ 1/2 mile to the SW, a small pond (less than 1 acre) ~ 300 yards to the NE, pools in an intermittent stream ~ 600 yards to the north and a small pond ~ 3 acres in size 3/4 mile to the southeast (east of Riverside Road & immediately south of a medical complex on Corporate Drive).  Temperatures last night reached the low to mid-30s with a cold wet rain (1/2 to 1" locally).  I suspect the bird may have become grounded and/or stressed by the weather and/or confused by light reflecting off of the wet pavement in the nearby parking lot less than 2/10ths mile to the SW.  Another birder reported checking the site at 3 p.m. & was unable to relocate the limpkin.

Both birds flew away after a brief period in the area of the crotch. We moved away to not provoke the bird any longer.

Media notes: Juvenile moulting into second cycle basic plumage. Note replaced basic chest feathers with fine dark streaks and richer overall colour.
Observation Details: Adult perched on wire, balancing a wobbly wobble into the wind, took flight as we approached but immediately banked to perch again so set the trap a short way down. It flew immediately to sit above with interest, dropping down onto the very center. At this moment a second bird out of the sky was descending slowly yet eagerly, feet slightly extended. It didn't land but banked and continued to watch from a controlled, low arc over the field. The bird on the trap wasn't properly caught as we approached and flew off, but it came back around in a tight circle so we rolled past. Just moments later this second bird swooped in and was caught.   Banded 2207 02005. Undergoing a second prebasic moult! P1^2 and P2^1, perfectly symmetric. No signs of moult among tertials on either wing. Three breast feathers newly replaced basic, as well as a dozen or so scapulars. Fluffy gaps throughout back and crown suggested active body moult, but could only locate one pin on the capital tract amidst all of the fluff.
